:::{#exm-adjusted-r-squared}
#### Adjusted coefficient of determination of nested `mtcars` models

The `mtcars` data set has the fuel economy `mpg` of 32 cars from the 1974 *Motor Trend* magazine.
This example fits four nested linear models of `mpg`,
each adding one predictor to the one before,
and computes @def-adjusted-r-squared from its formula.

```{r}
#| label: adjusted-r-squared-mtcars
mtcars_formulas <- list(
  mpg ~ wt,
  mpg ~ wt + hp,
  mpg ~ wt + hp + qsec,
  mpg ~ wt + hp + qsec + drat
)
mtcars_fits <- lapply(mtcars_formulas, lm, data = mtcars)
mtcars_full_sigma2 <- summary(mtcars_fits[[4]])$sigma^2

mtcars_tss <- sum((mtcars$mpg - mean(mtcars$mpg))^2)
mtcars_criteria <- tibble::tibble(
  predictors = 1:4,
  r_squared = vapply(mtcars_fits, \(f) summary(f)$r.squared, numeric(1)),
  adj_r_squared = vapply(
    mtcars_fits,
    \(f) {
      df <- nrow(mtcars) - length(coef(f))
      1 - (sum(resid(f)^2) / df) / (mtcars_tss / (nrow(mtcars) - 1))
    },
    numeric(1)
  )
)
mtcars_criteria
```

The coefficient of determination $R^2$ never falls as a predictor is added,
and here it rises from `r round(mtcars_criteria$r_squared[1], 3)` to `r round(mtcars_criteria$r_squared[4], 3)`.
The adjusted coefficient of determination rises more slowly,
from `r round(mtcars_criteria$adj_r_squared[1], 3)` to `r round(mtcars_criteria$adj_r_squared[4], 3)`,
because each added predictor costs a degree of freedom.
It is largest for the model with `r which.max(mtcars_criteria$adj_r_squared)` predictors.
Its formula matches the `adj.r.squared` that `summary()` reports:
`r isTRUE(all.equal(mtcars_criteria$adj_r_squared, vapply(mtcars_fits, \(f) summary(f)$adj.r.squared, numeric(1))))`.

:::
